CHAPTER V
UNAVOIDABLE ADVERSE ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS
Some unavoidable adverse environmental effects would occur from mining operations despite efforts utilized to mitigate them. Inasmuch as mining at the high level rate of production (26 mtpy) is an extension of the proposed low level of development (19 mtpy) the adverse effects from the higher level of production can be expected to be greater in some instances.
Air Quality
Despite control measures employed by Westmoreland Resources within the mining area, air quality degradation will result during unfavorable periods of dryness and high winds. Personnel employed at the mine and persons residing downwind (northeasterly, easterly and southeasterly) from Tracts II and III will be most adversely affected. Even though dust control will be required within the mining area, there will be degradation of air quality along new and heavily travelled roads. Air quality degradation can be expected to be greater at the high level of production (26 mtpy) due to the utilization of more equipment on the mine site and haul roads. Even with sprinkling, the dust problem and its effects on plants could be substantial. Although deer and other wildlife are observed frequently on the mine area it is likely that wildlife and livestock would be far enough removed to breath dust only occasionally. When reclamation is initiated following mining an unavoidable 1-2 year lapse will occur in developing vegetative cover and during which unstabilized soil surfaces will contribute to suspended particulate concentrations.
